title: Antidepressant use and risk of adverse outcomes in older people: population based cohort study
authors: Coupland C, Dhiman P, Morriss R, Arthur A, Barton G, Hippisley-Cox J
followUp: new depression diagnoses from 1996 to 2007, followed to 31 December 2008; absolute risks estimated at 1 year
population: Patients aged 65 to 100 years with a new diagnosis of depression in 570 UK general practices contributing to the QResearch database
funder: This project was funded by the NIHR Health Technology Assessment Programme (project number 06/42/01).
authorConflicts: JH-C is director of QResearch, a not-for-profit venture between the University of Nottingham and EMIS, and director of ClinRisk Ltd; RM received support for speaking at pharmaceutical-sponsored meetings about non-drug treatment of depression and bipolar disorder.
result: Adjusted hazard ratios for SSRIs against no antidepressant use: falls 1.66 (95% CI 1.58 to 1.73; 3575 events), fracture 1.58 (1.48 to 1.68), all-cause mortality 1.54 (1.48 to 1.59), attempted suicide or self-harm 2.16 (1.71 to 2.71), stroke or TIA 1.17 (1.10 to 1.26), epilepsy or seizures 1.83 (1.49 to 2.26). Adjusted absolute risks over 1 year without antidepressants against sertraline: falls 3.46% against 5.57%, fracture 1.76% against 2.80%, all-cause mortality 7.04% against 10.20%, seizures 0.21% against 0.55%, stroke or TIA 2.23% against 2.70%, adverse drug reactions 0.26% against 0.42%. For most outcomes, risks were highest in the first 28 days of use and the first 28 days after stopping; the authors suggest that the rise after stopping may reflect illness or admission to hospital or a residential home that prompted stopping. Observational design susceptible to confounding by indication, channelling bias and residual confounding.
